analysis.one_liner: Imposes a seven-day waiting period and police background check before handgun sales.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the handgun waiting-period bill with 152 bipartisan cosponsors, but the House never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill made it illegal for licensed gun dealers to hand over a handgun until seven days had passed and the buyer's local police chief or sheriff had been notified and had no record that the buyer was legally barred from owning one. Buyers with imminent threats against them, holders of qualifying state permits, and residents of states that already ran their own waiting period or police check were exempt. The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee but never got a vote on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people at risk of gun violence, especially victims of domestic threats and people buying handguns from strangers, because the week-long pause gives police time to catch legally barred buyers — convicted felons, fugitives, drug addicts, people with certain mental-health commitments, and people in the country illegally — before the gun changes hands.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Requires licensed dealers, manufacturers, and importers to notify the buyer's chief local law enforcement officer within one day of a proposed handgun sale and wait seven days before delivering the gun, giving police a window to identify prohibited buyers.

Bans transfers to anyone police flag as barred under federal, state, or local law, and requires the buyer to sign a sworn statement under penalty of law that they are not a convicted felon, fugitive, drug user or addict, adjudicated mentally defective, illegal alien, dishonorably discharged service member, or renounced citizen.

Exempts people facing a documented threat to their own or a family member's life, holders of state permits issued within the past year after police verification, and buyers in states that already impose their own seven-day waiting period or police verification.

Protects privacy by requiring police to destroy the buyer's sworn statement within 30 days unless the transaction appears illegal, and bars dealers from disclosing information from police reports except to the buyer, law enforcement, or a court.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers face new paperwork and a week's delay on every sale, with fines up to $1,000 and up to a year in prison for violations; handgun buyers wait a week; local police departments take on the work of receiving statements and checking the buyer's status, though the bill expressly does not force them to act.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun dealers, buyers, and local police

drawbacks.text: The check depends on local police acting voluntarily: the bill states nothing in it 'shall be interpreted to require any action by a chief law enforcement officer,' so a police department that did nothing would simply let the sale proceed after seven days.
Police must destroy the buyer's sworn statement within 30 days unless the transaction looks illegal, which limits the system's ability to build records or catch repeat problems.

Opponents argued a one-week delay burdens law-abiding buyers — including people who feel they need a gun for protection — without stopping determined criminals, who can get guns through illegal channels that never touch a licensed dealer.
The threat exception lets a buyer skip the waiting period entirely by obtaining an officer's statement that they face a danger to their household, a channel open to abuse.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The waiting period is a modest, paper-based intervention: it costs lawful buyers a week and dealers some paperwork, and its teeth depend on police departments choosing to run the checks. Even taking those limits seriously, the burden on ordinary people is small and temporary, while the chance to stop a legally prohibited buyer before delivery is a real public-safety gain.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee approved it in September 1990 and it was placed on the House calendar, but the House never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 4, 1989 by Rep. Edward Feighan of Ohio with 27 original cosponsors and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
It sat in the Crime Subcommittee for over a year, with hearings in April 1989, before the subcommittee forwarded it to the full committee in amended form in June 1990.
The full Judiciary Committee amended and reported it on September 10, 1990 as H. Rept. 101-691, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the queue of bills ready for House floor action.
The bill gathered 152 cosponsors, including 21 House Republicans, but no floor vote ever came, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Licensed gun dealers and handgun buyers avoided a federal seven-day waiting period and police notification requirement, and the gun-rights lobby avoided a federal check it had fought against. People at risk of gun violence got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers and the gun lobby

for.name: Rep. Edward F. Feighan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 4, 1989 and recruited cosponsors across two years.

for.name: 152 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including 131 of 257 House Democrats and 21 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support well beyond the sponsor.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings, amended the bill in subcommittee and full committee, and reported it to the House in September 1990.

against.what_they_did: Fought the Brady waiting period in Congress during this era, the central organized opposition to the bill.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote despite its committee approval and place on the calendar.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 131 of 257 House Democrats and 21 of 175 House Republicans cosponsored, and the bill never reached a recorded vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a seven-day hold and a police-notification step on every handgun sale by a licensed dealer, with fines up to $1,000 and up to a year in prison for violations. Because the bill died, dealers kept selling with no waiting period and no background check.

Police chiefs and sheriffs would have received sworn statements from handgun buyers and been asked to check for legal bars, adding workload, and the bill explicitly imposed no duty to act. Their interest ran with the public's, since the check helps them intercept illegal sales.
